title: Divorce and Children
text:
By the late 1980s, divorce had become common in the United States, and the question of how it affects children was the subject of heated debate. Some studies found serious harm; others found almost none. In 1991, the sociologists Paul Amato and Bruce Keith brought order to the evidence with a meta-analysis that combined the results of 92 studies involving more than 13,000 children.

On average, children whose parents had divorced did somewhat worse than children in intact families on a range of measures: school achievement, conduct, psychological adjustment, self-esteem and relationships with others. But the differences were small, and many studies had found larger effects than the better-designed, more recent ones.

A key comparison concerned conflict. Children who lived in intact families with high levels of conflict between their parents had lower well-being than children of divorce. In other words, the fighting between parents seemed to matter at least as much as the separation itself. The quality of the child's relationship with both parents after the divorce, and the economic hardship that often followed, also made a difference.

The study helped shift attention from the question of whether parents divorce to how they handle conflict and care for their children, whether married or not.
lesson: Ongoing conflict between parents can hurt children as much as separation itself. Whether together or apart, keep children out of the battlefield.
source: Amato, P. R., and Keith, B. (1991). Parental divorce and the well-being of children: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 110(1), 26-46.
